name: BoolQ
description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer (yes or no). Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and paired with Wikipedia passages. The dataset contains 16,000 questions split into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set.
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
publisher: University of Washington and Google AI Language
citeAs: Clark, C., Lee, K., Chang, M.-W., Kwiatkowski, T., Collins, M., & Toutanova, K. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044.
rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. The question and Wikipedia page are then given to a human annotator for further processing. Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) deciding if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, requesting factual information), (2) finding a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, and (3) marking whether the answer is yes or no. 13k questions were gathered from this pipeline and combined with 3k yes/no questions from the NQ training set.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators can mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information. Only questions marked as having a yes/no answer are used.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine paired with Wikipedia pages returned as one of the first five search results. Additionally, 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set were incorporated.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: 13k questions gathered from the Google search/Wikipedia pipeline were combined with an additional 3k questions with yes/no answers from the NQ training set to reach a total of 16k questions. These were split into a 3.2k dev set, 3.2k test set, and 9.4k train set, ensuring questions from NQ are always in the train set.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length are selected as likely yes/no questions. Only questions where a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results are kept. Questions marked as not good or not answerable by annotators are excluded. Each question is paired with the selected passage instead of the entire document to reduce ambiguity and keep input size manageable.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process. First, they decide if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page. Next, for good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question. Finally, annotators mark whether the question's answer is 'yes' or 'no'. Annotation quality was assessed by having three of the authors label 110 randomly chosen examples; disagreements were resolved by mutual agreement to create gold-standard labels. The answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels. Since agreement was sufficiently high, singly-annotated examples were used in the training/dev/test sets.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. If there was a disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement (gold-standard labels). Answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels. Of the cases where annotations differed from gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 (singly-annotated examples used in training/dev/test sets; 110 examples were annotated by 3 authors for quality assessment)
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset has been noted to have been updated since the inference type analysis was carried out, suggesting ongoing maintenance. No formal versioning or deprecation policy is described.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions, which has real-world applications in question answering systems. The questions are naturally occurring, meaning they reflect genuine information needs of users.
rai:dataBiases: Yes answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). The dataset is noted to have a correlation between question topic/type and the likelihood of a yes answer, though this correlation is too weak to outperform the majority baseline. Questions from QuAC, a related dataset, are noted to be 80% yes answers, and heuristically extracted yes/no questions from MS Marco are also 80% yes answers.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset contains only yes/no questions and may not generalize to other question types. The question-type inference analysis may be slightly out-of-date as the dataset has been updated since that analysis was carried out. The dataset uses singly-annotated examples, which may introduce some label noise (estimated ~10% error rate based on quality assessment). The passages are from Wikipedia, which may not represent all domains.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, development, and testing of reading comprehension and natural language inference models, specifically for yes/no question answering. It can be used to evaluate a model's ability to make complex inferences from text. The authors also use it to study transfer learning from entailment, paraphrase, and extractive QA datasets.
